title: Health Checks: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes
lesson:
A health check is how infrastructure decides what to do with an instance. The key insight is that different questions need different checks. Liveness asks: is this process stuck beyond recovery, so it should be restarted? Readiness asks: can this instance usefully serve traffic right now, so it should be in the load balancer's rotation? Startup asks: has a slow-booting process finished initializing, so the other probes can begin?

Conflating liveness and readiness is a classic outage cause. If a liveness probe fails whenever a downstream database is slow, then a database blip makes the orchestrator restart every healthy instance at once, turning a partial degradation into a full outage. Liveness should check only the process itself (event loop responsive, not deadlocked). Dependency problems belong in readiness, where failing simply removes the instance from rotation without killing it.

Readiness checks need care too. A deep readiness check that verifies every dependency can cause all instances to go unready simultaneously when a shared dependency fails, leaving the service with no endpoints at all, even though some features (or cached data) could still have been served. Many teams keep readiness shallow, covering only dependencies the instance cannot function without, and rely on circuit breakers and timeouts for the rest. Load balancers also use thresholds (for example, N consecutive failures to mark unhealthy, M successes to mark healthy) to avoid flapping.

Startup probes exist because applications that warm caches or load large models may take minutes to boot. Without one, a liveness probe with a short timeout would kill the process repeatedly before it ever becomes healthy. A startup probe holds off liveness and readiness checks until it succeeds once, so the liveness timeout can stay tight for steady state.

questions.prompt: What should a failing readiness probe cause the orchestrator to do?
options: Remove the instance from the load balancer rotation without restarting it
questions.explanation: Readiness controls whether an instance receives traffic; restarting is the job of the liveness probe.

questions.prompt: It is a good practice for a liveness probe to fail whenever a downstream database is slow.
questions.explanation: Restarting healthy instances because of a shared dependency problem can cascade a degradation into a full outage.

questions.prompt: A ____ probe delays liveness and readiness checks until a slow-booting application has finished initializing.
questions.explanation: The startup probe lets liveness stay tight for steady state without killing a process that is merely slow to boot.

questions.prompt: Why can a deep readiness check that verifies every dependency be dangerous?
options: If a shared dependency fails, all instances go unready at once and the service has no endpoints
questions.explanation: Simultaneous unreadiness removes all capacity even though some functionality might have continued working.

questions.prompt: Order the lifecycle of a slow-starting instance behind a load balancer, earliest first.
items: Readiness probe passes and the instance receives traffic
questions.explanation: The process boots, the startup probe gates the other probes, liveness monitors it, and readiness admits it to rotation.
